beitzah-4a-18-19.note: Rav Pappa's host, or by another version a man who came before him, had eggs laid on a Shabbat that fell the day before a Festival, and asked whether he could eat them the next day, on the Festival. Rav Pappa told him to go and come back tomorrow; the Gemara explains that Rav would not give public rulings during Festival days because of drinking. When the man returned, Rav Pappa told him that if he had answered then, he would have forgotten and ruled with Rabbi Yohanan, but Rava had said the law follows Rav in these three issues, whether lenient or strict.
beitzah-4a-18-19.why: The Gemara has been discussing eggs laid on a day of rest and the dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yohanan about using them the next day; after Rav Adda's answer to his host, this similar case shows that here the law follows Rav.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who is asked about the eggs and delays his answer until the next day.

people.name: Rav
people.about: An earlier Sage whose practice and ruling Rav Pappa follows.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who disputes Rav; normally the law follows him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who said the law follows Rav in three such cases.

terms.meaning: A biblical holiday on which most work is forbidden, though cooking for that day is allowed.
A speaker who repeated and explained a Sage's teaching aloud to a large audience.
Jewish law; the binding ruling.

beitzah-5a-9-9.note: Rabbi Eliezer owned a fourth-year vineyard east of Lod near the village of Tavi, close enough to Jerusalem that its fruit had to be brought there rather than redeemed for money. Unable to bring it to the Temple, which had been destroyed, he wanted to declare the fruit ownerless for the poor. His students told him there was no need: his colleagues had already voted and permitted it. The Gemara identifies those colleagues as Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai.
beitzah-5a-9-9.why: Rav Yosef holds that a ban enacted by a vote needs another vote to lift it, even after its reason is gone. The Gemara points out that the Jerusalem rule ended only because the Sages voted, and applies this to the egg laid on a Festival, whose ban was never lifted.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Owner of the fourth-year vineyard, who wanted to give its fruit to the poor.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The colleague whose vote had already permitted redeeming such fruit.

terms.meaning: Fruit of a vine's fourth year was eaten in Jerusalem, or redeemed for money spent there; farms within a day's walk had to bring the fruit itself.
Fruit formally given up by its owner, which anyone, here the poor, may take.

beitzah-6b-11-11.note: A man went around asking, Who has eggs of a live chicken? He was given eggs taken from a slaughtered chicken. He came before Rabbi Ami, who told the sellers it was a mistaken transaction and the sale was cancelled.
beitzah-6b-11-11.why: The Gemara explains Rav's statement that an egg is complete only when it emerges: only a laid egg can hatch a chick. Asked what difference that makes, it answers buying and selling, and gives this sale as the example.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage who voids the sale.

terms.meaning: A sale based on a basic error about what was sold; it is cancelled entirely, not just adjusted by a refund.

beitzah-7a-2-2.note: A man asked the vendors whether anyone had eggs from a hen that had been with a rooster. They gave him eggs that had not been fertilized by a rooster. He came before Rabbi Ami, who told the sellers it was a mistaken transaction and the sale was cancelled.
beitzah-7a-2-2.why: The Gemara has explained that only a laid egg can hatch a chick, which matters for buying and selling; this second case of Rabbi Ami's follows the first. The Gemara says the ruling is needed because one might think the buyer only wanted richer eating eggs and was owed just the price difference.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage who voids the sale.

terms.meaning: A sale based on a basic error about what was sold; it is cancelled entirely, not just adjusted by a refund.

beitzah-9b-2-2.note: Rabbi Hiyya's sons went out to the villages. When they came back, their father asked whether any case needing a legal ruling had come up. They said they had been asked about carrying an attic ladder to a dovecote on a Festival, and had permitted it. Rabbi Hiyya told them: Go out and forbid what you permitted.
beitzah-9b-2-2.why: A teaching records Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel arguing over moving a dovecote ladder on a Festival, with Rabbi Yehuda adding that an attic ladder is forbidden to all. The Gemara explains the sons read Rabbi Yehuda as disagreeing with the first teacher, when he was only explaining him.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The father, who orders his sons to reverse their ruling.

people.name: the sons of Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: They ruled in the villages that an attic ladder could be carried to a dovecote.

terms.meaning: An ordinary household ladder with many uses, as opposed to one made just for a dovecote; carrying it on a Festival could look like weekday work.
A structure where doves were kept; a ladder was needed to reach the birds.

beitzah-9b-6-6.note: By another version, Rabbi Hiyya's sons told him they had been asked about tilting an attic ladder from one window of a dovecote to another on a Festival, and had permitted it. Rabbi Hiyya told them: Go out and forbid what you permitted. The Gemara explains that they thought Rabbi Dosa was more lenient than the first teacher and allowed even an attic ladder, when in fact he was stricter, allowing even a dovecote ladder only to be tilted.
beitzah-9b-6-6.why: The Gemara has just explained the first version of this incident; this second version moves the sons' mistake to Rabbi Dosa's ruling in the same teaching about ladders.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The father, who orders his sons to reverse their ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya's sons
people.about: They permitted tilting an attic ladder at a dovecote.

people.name: Rabbi Dosa
people.about: An earlier Sage whose ruling on tilting a ladder the sons misread.

terms.meaning: Leaning a ladder from one window to another without carrying it, a lighter act than moving it.
An ordinary household ladder, as opposed to one made just for a dovecote.

beitzah-14b-1-2.note: Rav Pappi came to Mar Shmuel's house on a Festival and was served porridge of wheat groats, but he did not eat it, worried the wheat had been pounded that day. The Gemara asks why he did not assume a small mortar and pestle had been used, which is allowed, and answers that he saw it was finely ground. Asked why he did not assume it had been prepared the day before, the Gemara answers that he saw the husks were bright, so it was fresh. Or, the Gemara offers, Mar Shmuel's house was different, since he had slaves, and slaves are lax about such prohibitions.
beitzah-14b-1-2.why: Two teachings disagree on whether a small mortar and pestle may be used on a Festival, and Rava said the lenient one is for Babylonia and the strict one for the Land of Israel, where people had servants. This visit tests that distinction in a Babylonian house that had slaves.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: The guest who would not eat the porridge.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The host whose household served it.

terms.meaning: Coarsely crushed grain; pounding grain on a Festival was restricted.
A bowl and club for crushing grain; a large one looks like weekday work.

beitzah-15b-9-12.note: Rabbi Eliezer sat lecturing on the laws of the Festival the whole Festival day. As groups left one after another, he called them owners of huge vats, then of barrels, jugs, jars and cups, and when a sixth group began to leave, owners of a curse. When he looked at the students who remained, their faces changed in shame. He told them: My sons, I did not mean you but those who left, who abandon eternal life for temporary life. When the remaining students left at the end, he sent them off with Nehemiah's verse: Go, eat the fat and drink the sweet, and send portions to whoever has nothing, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.
beitzah-15b-9-12.why: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer could fault the leavers when festival joy is itself a mitzva. It answers that he held festival joy optional: a Festival day should be all eating or all study, while Rabbi Yehoshua said to split it, half for God and half for yourselves.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage lecturing all day, who mocks the groups that leave and comforts the students who stay.

terms.meaning: A biblical holiday, such as Passover or Sukkot, meant for rest and celebration.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the mishna.

beitzah-16b-6-6.note: A blind man who recited mishnayot before Mar Shmuel looked sad. Mar Shmuel asked why, and he said he had not prepared a joining of cooked foods before the Festival. Mar Shmuel told him to rely on his. The next year he was sad again for the same reason. This time Mar Shmuel told him he was negligent: everyone else may rely on his joining, but not him.
beitzah-16b-6-6.why: The Gemara is asking whether a joining of cooked foods works only if the person it covers knows about it, citing Sages who made one for a whole city. This case shows one man's joining covering others, and its maker refusing to cover someone who was habitually negligent.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose joining of cooked foods covers others, and who refuses it to the blind man the second year.

people.name: the blind person
people.about: He recited mishnayot before Mar Shmuel and twice forgot to prepare his own joining.

terms.meaning: Called eiruv tavshilin: food set aside before a Festival that falls on Friday, which allows cooking on the Festival for Shabbat.
Teachings of the mishna, the early collection of Jewish law; some people's job was to recite them from memory.

beitzah-20a-11-12.note: Hillel the Elder brought a burnt-offering to the Temple courtyard on a Festival to place his hands on it. Shammai's students surrounded him and asked what animal it was. To avoid a quarrel, he told them it was a female, a peace-offering, and swung its tail so they could not tell, and they left. That day Beit Shammai gained the upper hand and sought to fix the law their way. But Bava ben Buta, an Elder among Shammai's disciples who knew the law followed Beit Hillel, brought all the fine sheep of Kedar in Jerusalem into the courtyard and invited anyone to place hands on them. That day Beit Hillel prevailed, and the law was fixed their way with no one disputing it.
beitzah-20a-11-12.why: The Gemara is working through Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's dispute over whether offerings may have hands placed on them on a Festival; this incident shows how Beit Hillel's view became the law.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: Founder of Beit Hillel; he hides the nature of his offering from Shammai's students to avoid a quarrel.

people.name: Bava ben Buta
people.about: An Elder among Shammai's disciples who knew the law followed Beit Hillel and brought sheep for everyone to use.

people.name: Shammai the Elder
people.about: Founder of Beit Shammai, whose students challenge Hillel.

terms.meaning: Before an offering was slaughtered, the owner pressed his hands on the animal's head.
A burnt-offering, always male, was burned whole on the altar; most of a peace-offering was eaten by its owners.
The schools of Shammai and Hillel, who argue over many laws.
Fine sheep named for a region known for its flocks.

beitzah-20b-1-1.note: Some time later, a disciple of Beit Hillel brought his burnt-offering to the Temple courtyard to place his hands on it on a Festival. A disciple of Beit Shammai found him and asked, What is this placing of hands? He answered, What is this silence? meaning that since the law was not fixed their way, the other should keep quiet. He silenced him with this rebuke, and the Beit Shammai disciple left.
beitzah-20b-1-1.why: This follows the story of Bava ben Buta, after which the law on placing hands was fixed by Beit Hillel. Abaye learns from the exchange that a scholar who is reproached should not answer back with more than was said to him.

people.name: a disciple of Beit Hillel
people.about: He brings a burnt-offering and places his hands on it on a Festival.

people.name: a disciple of Beit Shammai
people.about: He challenges the placing of hands and is silenced.

terms.meaning: Before an offering was slaughtered, the owner pressed his hands on the animal's head.
An offering burned entirely on the altar.
The schools of Shammai and Hillel, who argue over many laws.

beitzah-21a-1-2.note: Rav Avya the Elder asked Rav Huna whether an animal owned half by a gentile and half by a Jew may be slaughtered on a Festival. Rav Huna said it may. Rav Avya asked how that differs from vow-offerings and gift-offerings, which may not be slaughtered on a Festival. Rav Huna said to him: Look, a raven flies. After Rav Avya left, Rav Huna's son Rabba asked his father why he had treated so great a man that way. Rav Huna answered that he was worn out, quoting Song of Songs, and the question needed careful reasoning.
beitzah-21a-1-2.why: Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai argue over which offerings may be slaughtered on a Festival, and vow- and gift-offerings are forbidden. After this exchange the Gemara gives the answer Rav Huna did not: the gentile's half does not matter, but offerings are eaten at the table of the Most High.

people.name: Rav Avya the Elder
people.about: The Sage who asks Rav Huna the question.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who answers briefly and then dodges the follow-up.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Rav Huna's son, who asks his father why he treated Rav Avya that way.

terms.meaning: Voluntary offerings brought by choice, not on a fixed day; part goes on the altar and part is eaten by the owner and priests.
A biblical holiday on which most work is forbidden, though slaughtering and cooking food for that day is allowed.

beitzah-21a-11-12.note: Shimon the Timnite did not come to the study hall on the night of the Festival. In the morning Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava asked him why. He said a military search unit had come to their town wanting to pillage it, so they slaughtered a calf, fed the soldiers and sent them off in peace. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava said he wondered whether their gain was not outweighed by their loss, since the Torah allows food to be prepared on a Festival only for you, and not for gentiles.
beitzah-21a-11-12.why: Rav Huna has ruled that villagers may bake bread for troops on a Festival if a Jewish child could eat some of it; the Gemara brings this incident against him, since the calf could also have been eaten by Jews and yet it was condemned.

people.name: Shimon the Timnite
people.about: He missed the study hall because his town slaughtered a calf on the Festival to feed soldiers.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: The Sage who questions Shimon and condemns what the town did.

terms.meaning: The house of study where Sages and students learned Torah together.
The Torah's words about Festival cooking, read to mean food for Jews, not for gentiles.

beitzah-22a-5-5.note: Ulla came to visit Rav Yehuda on a Festival, and Ulla's servant tilted the oil lamp so that the oil would run away from the wick and the light would go out sooner. Rav Yehuda challenged Ulla with a teaching that anyone who takes oil from a burning lamp is guilty of extinguishing it. Ulla agreed and answered that his servant had done it without his knowledge.
beitzah-22a-5-5.why: The Gemara is discussing the mishna's rule that a fallen candelabrum may not be set up on a Festival; this lamp incident opens a series of rulings on what counts as putting out a light on a Festival.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A Sage visiting Rav Yehuda's house; his servant tilted the lamp.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The host, who objects that tilting the lamp is a form of extinguishing.

terms.meaning: One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot. Most work forbidden on Shabbat is forbidden on these days too, except work needed to prepare food.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core legal code the Talmud discusses.
Putting out a fire is one of the kinds of work forbidden on Shabbat; the teaching says even making a lamp burn out sooner counts as doing it.

beitzah-22b-10-11.note: A teaching reports that the house of Rabban Gamliel swept the dining room and put incense on coals on a Festival, though others did not. Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok said he had often gone with his father into Rabban Gamliel's house and seen how it was really done. The room was swept the day before and covered with sheets, and the sheets were lifted when the guests arrived, so the house was found clean on its own. In the same way, iron coal pans were filled with fragrant smoke the day before and plugged, then opened when the guests came, so the house was perfumed on its own. The other Sages answered that if so, this would be allowed even on Shabbat.
beitzah-22b-10-11.why: Rav Asi had said the dispute over incense was only about perfuming clothes; the Gemara cites this account to challenge him, since the Sages' reply implies even incense for its smell is forbidden, and it then reverses his statement.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Leader whose household practices on the Festival are described.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok
people.about: Eyewitness who often went with his father into Rabban Gamliel's house.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's father, whom he followed into Rabban Gamliel's house.

terms.meaning: A collection of early rabbinic teachings arranged alongside the Mishna, the core legal code the Talmud discusses.
The dining room, where people reclined on couches to eat.
One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which most work is forbidden except work needed to prepare food.

beitzah-23a-5-5.note: Rabbi Yosei reports that Theodosius of Rome, a leader of the Jews there, set up a custom for the Roman Jews to eat a whole roasted kid goat on the night of Passover, as was done with the Passover offering in the Temple. The Sages sent him a message: were you not Theodosius, we would have decreed ostracism on you, because you are feeding the Jewish people consecrated food outside the Temple.
beitzah-23a-5-5.why: The mishna lists preparing a whole kid on Passover night as one of Rabban Gamliel's leniencies, which the Rabbis forbid; this report shows the Sages' objection, and the Gemara then explains they meant the meat only looked like a Temple offering.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Theodosius of Rome
people.about: Leader of the Jewish community in Rome who started the custom.

terms.meaning: A young goat roasted whole, with its innards placed over its head, the way the Passover lamb was roasted in the Temple.
A formal ban by the Sages that cut a person off from normal dealings with the community.
Meat of offerings dedicated to the Temple, which may be eaten only in and around the Temple itself.

beitzah-25b-11-12.note: Rav Nahman asked Hama bar Adda, a messenger who traveled between Babylonia and the Land of Israel, to go out of his way to the Ladder of Tyre and ask Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi what the rule was for being carried in a chair on a Festival. By the time he got there, Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi had died. Instead he found Rabbi Zerika, who told him that Rabbi Ami allowed it, provided the person is not carried on the shoulders. Rav Yosef, son of Rabba, explained that this means on poles resting on the bearers' shoulders.
beitzah-25b-11-12.why: A teaching forbids going out in a carried chair on a Festival, yet Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi had reported that it was allowed for a man the public needed; Rav Nahman wanted the rule from him directly.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage in Babylonia who sends the question.

people.name: Hama bar Adda
people.about: Messenger of the academies who carried the question to the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi
people.about: Sage in Tyre to whom the question was addressed; he died before it reached him.

people.name: Rabbi Zerika
people.about: Sage who answered instead, quoting Rabbi Ami.

people.name: Rav Yosef, son of Rabba
people.about: Sage who explained what 'not carried on the shoulders' means.

terms.meaning: A steep coastal pass near the city of Tyre, on a roundabout route into the Land of Israel.
One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which ordinary weekday activity is restricted.
A seat carried by bearers, like a litter; using one looked like a weekday activity.

beitzah-27a-5-5.note: A man in Babylonia, whose name is not given, wished that he might go up to the Land of Israel and hear a ruling from the mouth of the Sage who taught it. When he got there he found Rabbi Zeira and asked him whether he had really said that the law follows Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Zeira said no: what he had said was only that it stands to reason.
beitzah-27a-5-5.why: The Gemara is debating whether a firstborn animal's blemish may be examined on a Festival; Rabbi Abba had claimed Rabbi Zeira ruled like Rabbi Shimon, and this trip checks that report at its source.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Sage in the Land of Israel whose reported ruling the traveler came to check.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Earlier Sage whose opinion on the question was said to be the law.

terms.meaning: Rabbi Zeira's way of saying his view was his own reasoning, not a received tradition that the law is so.

beitzah-27a-14-14.note: Ami of Vardina examined firstborn animals for the household of the Nasi, but on Festivals he would not examine them. When Rabbi Ami was told, he said Ami did well. The Gemara objects that Rabbi Ami himself examined firstborns, and answers that he looked at the blemish the day before and on the Festival only asked how it happened. So it was with Rava: a man brought him a firstborn near nightfall on the eve of a Festival while Rava was washing his hair. Rava looked up, saw the blemish, and told him to come back tomorrow. The next day Rava asked how it happened; the owner said barley lay on the far side of a thorn fence and the animal cut its lip reaching for it. Rava asked if he had caused it, and he said no. The text does not say what Rava then ruled.
beitzah-27a-14-14.why: The Gemara has been discussing the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda over examining firstborn blemishes on a Festival; right after, it explains why Rava asked whether the owner caused the blemish, since causing one is forbidden.

people.name: Ami of Vardina
people.about: Examiner of firstborn animals for the household of the Nasi, who would not examine them on Festivals.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who approved of Ami of Vardina's practice.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage before whom a firstborn was brought on the eve of a Festival.

terms.meaning: A male firstborn calf, lamb or kid belonged to a priest as an offering. If it had a permanent blemish, an expert could declare it fit to be slaughtered and eaten as ordinary meat.
The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel.
One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot.

beitzah-28a-5-5.note: Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, used to divide meat between them on a Festival by weighing one portion against the other on a scale. The text tells nothing more of the incident.
beitzah-28a-5-5.why: The mishna forbids weighing meat on a Festival, with Rabbi Yehuda allowing it only against a vessel or cleaver; the Gemara asks whose view these two followed, and answers that it was Rabbi Yehoshua, who allows weighing portion against portion.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Sage who divided meat with Rabbi Shimon on a Festival.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who shared the meat with Rabbi Hiyya.

terms.meaning: One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which weekday business practices like weighing goods are restricted.

beitzah-28a-19-19.note: Rav Nehemya, son of Rav Yosef, recalled standing before Rava on a Festival while Rava ran a knife over the rim of a basket. He asked whether Rava was sharpening it or cleaning off the fat. Rava said he was removing the fat, but Rav Nehemya could tell he was really sharpening it. He held that sharpening was allowed, but that this should not be taught as a public ruling.
beitzah-28a-19-19.why: Shmuel taught that a knife may be run over another only to clean it, not to sharpen it, while Rava had just credited Rav Hisda with ruling like Rabbi Yehuda, who allows tasks that make food preparation possible; this shows Rava following that ruling quietly.

people.name: Rav Nehemya, son of Rav Yosef
people.about: Student who watched Rava and tells the story.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who ran a knife over a basket rim on a Festival.

terms.meaning: One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which work is restricted except what is needed to prepare food.

terms.term: the halakha, but a ruling is not issued
terms.meaning: A rule that is correct in law but that Sages would not announce publicly, so that people would not take it too far.

beitzah-28b-1-1.note: Abaye recalled standing before his teacher Rabba on a Festival while Rabba ran a knife over the edge of a millstone. Abaye asked whether he meant to sharpen it or to clean off the fat. Rabba said to remove the fat, but Abaye could tell he was sharpening it. Rabba held that sharpening was allowed, but that this should not be taught as a public ruling.
beitzah-28b-1-1.why: This follows Rav Nehemya's almost identical account of Rava; the two reports together show leading Sages quietly following Rabbi Yehuda's lenient view on sharpening a knife on a Festival.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Student who watched his teacher and tells the story.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Abaye's master and teacher, who ran a knife over a millstone on a Festival.

terms.meaning: One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which work is restricted except what is needed to prepare food.

terms.term: the halakha, but a ruling is not issued
terms.meaning: A rule that is correct in law but that Sages would not announce publicly, so that people would not take it too far.

beitzah-29a-10-13.note: Abba Shaul ben Botnit, a Sage who was also a grocer, would fill his measures on the eve of a Festival and hand them to customers on the Festival; he did the same on the intermediate days so as not to lose time in the study hall. He gathered three hundred jugs of wine from the foam of his measures, which he felt he had not earned, and his colleagues gathered three hundred jugs of oil from what was left in their measures. They brought them to the Temple treasurers in Jerusalem, who said they need not do this. They said they did not want it. The treasurers told them to use it for communal needs, which Rav Hisda explains as cisterns, ditches and caves for water.
beitzah-29a-10-13.why: The mishna on measuring goods for a Festival cites Abba Shaul's practice, and the Gemara has just explained how Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis treat filling a measuring vessel; the baraita adds more about the man and his scruples.

people.name: Abba Shaul ben Botnit
people.about: A Sage and grocer, careful not to profit from anything that was not his.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Sage who explains what 'communal needs' means.

terms.meaning: The middle days of Passover and Sukkot, when some work is permitted but the days are still part of the holiday.
Officials in Jerusalem who received and managed funds and goods given to the Temple.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core legal code the Talmud discusses.
Public works for everyone's benefit, used to repay a theft when the victims cannot be identified.

beitzah-29b-4-4.note: Rav Yosef's wife was sifting flour on the back side of a sieve. He told her: look, I want good bread, a hint that she could sift in the normal way. Rav Ashi's wife was sifting flour onto a table. Rav Ashi said that his wife was the daughter of Rami bar Hama, a man careful in his deeds, and she would not do this had she not seen it in her father's house.
beitzah-29b-4-4.why: The Gemara is debating whether flour may be sifted a second time on a Festival; Rav Nahman has said every woman in Neharde'a already does it, and these two households show how it was done in practice.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who tells his wife she may sift flour normally.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who trusts his wife's practice, learned in her father's house.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: Rav Ashi's father-in-law, called a master of good deeds.

terms.meaning: Sifting with the sieve upside down, an unusual way of doing it that marks the work as different from an ordinary weekday.

beitzah-32b-2-3.note: Rav Natan bar Abba, quoting Rav, said the wealthy Jews of Babylonia will go down to Gehenna. He illustrates it with Shabbetai bar Marinus, who came to Babylonia and asked the wealthy there to invest with him in a business venture; they refused. He asked them for food to live on, and they refused that too. He said they must descend from the mixed multitude, because anyone who has compassion for others is known to be a descendant of Abraham, and anyone who does not, is not.
beitzah-32b-2-3.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav Natan bar Abba on trimming a lamp wick, and so gathers his other teachings together to make them easier to remember; this is one of them.

people.name: Rav Natan bar Abba
people.about: Sage who reports Rav's saying about the wealthy of Babylonia.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage whose harsh saying about the wealthy is quoted.

people.name: Shabbetai bar Marinus
people.about: A visitor to Babylonia refused both an investment and food by the wealthy there.

terms.meaning: The place of punishment for the wicked after death.
The non-Israelites who left Egypt with the Israelites in the Exodus, not descendants of Abraham.
A partnership in which an investor lends money and shares the profits.

beitzah-36b-3-4.note: Abaye's millhouse sprang a leak on Shabbat, and he came to his teacher Rabba for advice. Rabba told him to bring his bed into the millhouse, so the dirty water would count like a container of excrement in his living space, which may be carried out, and then to remove it. Abaye sat and puzzled over whether one may create such a situation on purpose. Meanwhile his millhouse collapsed. Abaye said: I had this coming for going against my master.
beitzah-36b-3-4.why: A teaching has just allowed a vessel placed under a leak on Shabbat to be emptied and put back again; this case asks what one may do when that is not enough to handle the water.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Owner of the leaking millhouse, and Rabba's student.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who tells him how to get rid of the water.

terms.meaning: Something so repulsive that, although normally it may not be moved on Shabbat, the Sages let a person carry it out of the room where he is.
Items that may not be moved or handled on Shabbat because they are not meant for use that day.
The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest on which many kinds of work are forbidden.

beitzah-38a-8-8.note: When Rabbi Abba went up from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, he prayed that he would say something there that would be accepted. He found a group of leading Sages asking why the water and salt a woman borrows are not simply absorbed into her dough. Rabbi Abba said: if a man's one measure of wheat got mixed into another's ten, would the other man just eat it all and be glad? They laughed at him. He said: did I take your cloaks, that you laugh at me? They laughed at him again.
beitzah-38a-8-8.why: The mishna rules that a dough made with a neighbor's water and salt may be carried on a Festival only where both women may walk; the Sages asked why those small ingredients still count, and afterward Rabbi Oshaya says they were right to laugh while Rav Safra defends Rabbi Abba.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Sage newly arrived from Babylonia who hoped his words would be accepted.

terms.meaning: On a Festival an object may be carried only as far as its owner may walk; an item belonging to two people is limited by both.
When a small amount of something is mixed into a much larger amount, the law can treat the small part as if it has disappeared into the larger.
A measure of volume for grain and other dry goods.

beitzah-40a-8-8.note: Rav Hana bar Hanilai hung meat on the bar of his host's door while away from his own town on a Festival, and then asked whether he could take it home. He came before Rav Huna, who told him: if you hung it yourself, go and take it; if they hung it for you, do not take it.
beitzah-40a-8-8.why: Rav holds that an item left in someone's house follows the keeper's travel limits unless a corner was set aside for the owner; the Gemara asks how Rav Huna, Rav's student, could rule this way, and answers that a door bar counts as such a corner.

people.name: Rav Hana bar Hanilai
people.about: Sage who hung his meat at his host's house and asked whether he could take it.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Sage who gave him the ruling.

terms.meaning: Here, a legal device that lets a person walk beyond the usual limit outside his town on Shabbat or a Festival.
One of the biblical holy days, such as Passover or Sukkot, on which there are limits on how far a person and his belongings may travel.
